exp_1_1_titel: How do you make a bulb light up?
exp_1_1_frage: In front of you are a battery, a bulb and some wires. Is one single wire from the battery to the bulb enough to make it light up?
exp_1_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp_1_1_s1: Drag a bulb from the parts tray onto fields A1 and A2.
exp_1_1_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to A1. Switch on the main switch. Does the bulb light up?
exp_1_1_s3: Now draw a black wire from A2 to 0V. What happens?
exp_1_1_h1: The current needs a way there and a way back.
exp_1_1_h2: Both ends of the bulb must be connected to the battery.
exp_1_1_loesung: One wire from +9V to A1, a second one from A2 to 0V – and switch on the main switch.
exp_1_1_erklaerung: Current only flows in a loop: from the battery through the bulb and back to the battery. If part of the path is missing, the loop is open and nothing lights up. That is why it is called an electric circuit.
exp_1_1_mehr: Here the battery is set to 4.5 V. The bulb is made for 6 V, so it glows a little dimmer. A bulb lights up because its very thin wire gets very hot.
exp_1_1_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. How bright is the bulb now?
exp_1_1_w2: Swap the two wires at the bulb. Does it still light up?
exp_1_1_echt: With a flat battery (4.5 V), a bulb from the craft shop and two wires, you can build this circuit for real.
exp_1_2_frage: A doorbell only rings while someone presses the button. Where does the push button have to go so that your buzzer works the same way?
exp_1_2_v1: The push button belongs in the path of the current to the buzzer.
exp_1_2_v2: The push button can be anywhere next to it.
exp_1_2_s1: Put the push button on fields A2 and A3.
exp_1_2_s2: Put the buzzer on A3 and A4. Its plus leg goes to A3.
exp_1_2_s3: Draw a red wire from +9V to A2 and a black one from A4 to 0V. Switch on and press the button!
exp_1_2_h1: A push button is a bridge that only holds while you press it.
exp_1_2_h2: The push button and the buzzer must be one after the other in the same circuit.
exp_1_2_loesung: +9V to A2, push button from A2 to A3, buzzer from A3 to A4 (plus at A3), A4 to 0V. Main switch on, then hold the push button down.
exp_1_2_erklaerung: The push button interrupts the circuit. When you press it, it closes the gap: current flows through the buzzer and it buzzes. When you let go, the circuit is open again. Parts placed one after the other like this form a series circuit.
exp_1_2_mehr: Inside your buzzer, a thin plate vibrates about 2400 times every second. You hear it as a high tone.
exp_1_2_w1: Put the push button somewhere else in the circuit, for example between the buzzer and 0V. Does it still ring?
exp_1_2_echt: With a 4.5 V battery, a buzzer and a push button, you can build a doorbell for your bedroom door.
exp_1_3_titel: The panel switch makes the motor run
exp_1_3_frage: A push button only holds while you press it. A switch stays the way you set it. Which is better if a fan should run for a long time?
exp_1_3_v1: The switch, because it stays on.
exp_1_3_v2: The push button, because it is easier to press.
exp_1_3_s1: Put the motor on fields C1 and C3.
exp_1_3_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to the panel field S1 and a second one from S2 to C1.
exp_1_3_s3: Draw a black wire from C3 to 0V. Switch on the main switch and then the panel switch S.
exp_1_3_h1: The panel switch S has two fields: S1 and S2. The current has to pass through it.
exp_1_3_h2: The path of the current: +9V, switch S, motor, 0V.
exp_1_3_loesung: +9V to S1, S2 to C1, motor from C1 to C3, C3 to 0V. Then switch on the main switch and the panel switch S.
exp_1_3_erklaerung: A switch keeps the circuit closed until you flip it back. So the motor runs without you having to press all the time. The main switch of the battery is also a switch like this.
exp_1_3_mehr: A motor turns electric current into a turning movement. The higher the voltage, the faster it turns.
exp_1_3_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V and then to 3 V. How does the motor change?
exp_1_3_w2: Swap the wires at C1 and C3. Which way does the motor turn now?
exp_1_3_echt: Many toys have small motors with a switch and batteries inside. Look where the switch is.
exp_2_4_titel: Why does the LED need a protector?
exp_2_4_frage: So far you have connected bulbs directly to the battery. Today you try an LED. It is much smaller and needs less current. Can you connect it just like a bulb?
exp_2_4_v1: Yes, it lights up the same way.
exp_2_4_v2: It shines brighter than the bulb.
exp_2_4_s1: Put the LED from B4 to C4. The long leg goes to B4. Draw a red wire from +9V to B4 and a black one from C4 to 0V. Switch on!
exp_2_4_s2: Repair the LED with a tap. Put the resistor with the rings yellow, violet, brown from B3 to B4. Move the end of the red wire from B4 to B3. What happens now?
exp_2_4_h1: Think: what slows down the current when there is no bulb in the circuit?
exp_2_4_h2: Look at fields B3 and B4. Something is still missing there.
exp_2_4_loesung: The resistor goes between +9V and the LED: from B3 to B4.
exp_2_4_erklaerung: A bulb slows the current down by itself, because its thin wire makes the way hard. The LED hardly does that. Without a brake, so much current flows that it gets too hot. The resistor is its protector: it only lets through as much current as the LED can take.
exp_2_4_mehr: With 470 ohms, about (9 V − 1.9 V) / 470 Ω ≈ 15 mA flows. The LED can take 20 mA continuously.
exp_2_4_w1: Replace the resistor with one of 1 kΩ. Does the LED get brighter or darker?
exp_2_4_echt: Build the circuit with your experiment kit – but only with the resistor! A real LED cannot be repaired with a tap.
lex_gluehlampe: A bulb lights up because a very thin wire gets very hot.
lex_taster: A push button only closes the circuit while you press it.
lex_wechselschalter: A changeover switch connects its middle either to one terminal or to the other. That way you can switch a light from two places.
lex_reedkontakt: A reed switch is a switch inside a small glass tube. If you hold a magnet next to it, it closes.
lex_motor: A motor turns electric current into a turning movement.
lex_summer: A buzzer hums or beeps when current flows through it.
lex_widerstand: A resistor slows down the current. The colour rings tell you how much.
lex_led: An LED only lights up in one direction and always needs a series resistor.
lex_diode: A diode only lets current through in one direction – like a one-way street.
lex_kondensator: A capacitor stores electric charge for a short time.
lex_elko: An electrolytic capacitor has a plus and a minus pole. Plugged in the wrong way round, it breaks.
lex_fotowiderstand: A photoresistor lets more current through in light than in the dark.
lex_transistor: A transistor is a switch controlled by a small current. It sits on a small board with four feet: B and C at the top, E twice at the bottom – the two E feet are connected on the board.
lex_blinkmodul: The blinker module switches its output on and off again and again.
lex_tonmodul: The tone module makes a sound as long as its input gets current.
stufe_0_frage: How do I make something blink?
stufe_1_frage: When does the bulb light up?
stufe_2_frage: What happens if I add a second bulb?
stufe_3_frage: How much current is actually flowing?
stufe_4_frage: How can one current control another?
exp_1_1_b1: With one wire the bulb stayed dark; with two wires it lit up.
exp_1_1_b2: The bulb already lit up with one wire.
exp_1_2_b1: The buzzer only buzzed while I was pressing the button.
exp_1_2_b2: The buzzer buzzed all the time.
exp_1_3_b1: The motor kept running without me holding anything down.
exp_2_4_b1: Without a resistor the LED broke; with the resistor it lit up.
exp_2_4_b2: The LED lit up normally without a resistor.
exp_2_4_b3: The LED did not light up at all.
exp_0_1_frage: There is a blinker module in the module bar at the bottom. Do you think you can make a light blink in just a few steps?
exp_0_1_b2: The LED stays on all the time.
exp_0_1_b3: It blinks, but I don't know why.
exp_0_1_s1: Put the resistor from B3 to B4 and the red LED from B4 to C4 (long leg to B4).
exp_0_1_s2: Connect +9V to the plus of the blinker module (M1) and minus (M2) to 0V.
exp_0_1_s3: Draw a wire from +9V to B3 and one from C4 to the module output (M3). Switch on!
exp_0_1_h1: The module needs power itself: plus and minus must go to the battery.
exp_0_1_h2: The module output switches the LED's path to 0V on and off.
exp_0_1_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, C4 → M3. Main switch on.
exp_0_1_erklaerung: The blinker module is a little switch that keeps turning itself on and off. You'll find out later how it works – at the end of the learning path you'll even build such a blinker from single parts.
exp_0_1_mehr: The module switches about once per second.
exp_0_1_w1: Use a green LED instead of the red one. Does it blink the same way?
exp_0_1_echt: You can find blinking lights on bike lamps, building sites and smoke detectors. On your next walk, look out for everything that blinks.
exp_1_4_frage: A torch only lights up when you press the button. What do you need besides a battery and a bulb?
exp_1_4_v1: A push button in the circuit.
exp_1_4_b1: The bulb only lights while I press the button.
exp_1_4_b2: The bulb lights all the time.
exp_1_4_s1: Put the push button on A2 and A3 and the bulb on A3 and A4.
exp_1_4_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to A2 and a black one from A4 to 0V.
exp_1_4_s3: Switch on and press the button.
exp_1_4_h1: The button must be able to interrupt the current's path to the bulb.
exp_1_4_h2: Button and bulb lie one after the other between +9V and 0V.
exp_1_4_loesung: +9V → A2, button A2–A3, bulb A3–A4, A4 → 0V. Main switch on, press the button.
exp_1_4_erklaerung: The button is a gap in the circuit that you close with your finger. That's exactly how a torch button works.
exp_1_4_mehr: Many torches have a switch that stays on instead of a push button.
exp_1_4_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. How bright is your torch now?
exp_1_4_echt: Open up an old torch with an adult: can you find the battery, bulb and switch?
exp_1_5_frage: This bulb is made for 2.5 V. The battery is set to 3 V. Do they go together?
exp_1_5_v1: Yes, 3 V is close enough to 2.5 V.
exp_1_5_b1: The bulb shines brightly and stays intact.
exp_1_5_s1: Put a bulb on B2 and B3. Choose the rated voltage 2.5 V in the part menu.
exp_1_5_s2: Draw a wire from +9V to B2 and from B3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_1_5_h1: The rated voltage is shown at the bulb. A long press or right-click opens the menu.
exp_1_5_loesung: Bulb B2–B3 at 2.5 V, +9V → B2, B3 → 0V, battery 3 V, main switch on.
exp_1_5_erklaerung: A bulb can take a little more than its rated voltage, but not much more. 3 V on a 2.5 V bulb just makes it a bit brighter. Far too much voltage would burn through the thin wire.
exp_1_5_mehr: The rated voltage is the voltage a part is made for.
exp_1_5_w1: Use a 6 V bulb at 3 V. How bright is it?
exp_1_5_echt: Real bulbs have the voltage printed on them. Read it before you connect a bulb to a battery.
exp_1_6_titel: A fan at the push of a button
exp_1_6_frage: You want a little fan that only turns while you press. How do you build it?
exp_1_6_v1: With a push button in front of the motor.
exp_1_6_b1: The motor only turns while I press.
exp_1_6_b2: The motor turns all the time.
exp_1_6_s1: Put the button on A1 and A2 and the motor from A2 to A4.
exp_1_6_s2: Draw a wire from +9V to A1 and a black one from A4 to 0V. Switch on and press.
exp_1_6_h1: The motor is long: it needs two fields of distance.
exp_1_6_h2: Button and motor lie one after the other.
exp_1_6_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, motor A2–A4, A4 → 0V. Main switch on, press the button.
exp_1_6_erklaerung: Current can make not only light but also movement. The motor turns the current into rotation – but only as long as the button closes the circuit.
exp_1_6_mehr: Light, heat, movement and sound are the effects of current you experience in Volta.
exp_1_6_w1: Swap the two wires at the motor. Does it turn the other way now?
exp_1_6_echt: Small motors with buttons are in toy cars and mixers. Ask an adult whether you can look at one together.
exp_1_7_frage: In your room the light stays on when you flip the switch. Can the panel switch S do that with a bulb?
exp_1_7_v2: No, I have to press all the time.
exp_1_7_b1: The bulb stays on until I switch S off again.
exp_1_7_b2: The bulb goes out straight away.
exp_1_7_s1: Put a bulb on B1 and B2.
exp_1_7_s2: Draw wires: +9V to S1, S2 to B1, B2 to 0V.
exp_1_7_s3: Switch on the main switch and then S.
exp_1_7_h1: S1 and S2 are the two terminals of the panel switch.
exp_1_7_h2: The current flows: +9V, switch S, bulb, 0V.
exp_1_7_loesung: +9V → S1, S2 → B1, bulb B1–B2, B2 → 0V; main switch and S on.
exp_1_7_erklaerung: A switch remembers its position. That's why the light stays on until you turn it off – just like the light switch in your room.
exp_1_7_mehr: Push button: only while you press. Switch: stays the way you set it.
exp_1_7_w1: Replace the bulb with the buzzer. What changes?
exp_1_7_echt: At home, count how many switches and how many push buttons (like the doorbell) you can find.
exp_2_1_titel: Two bulbs one after the other
exp_2_1_frage: What happens if you connect two bulbs one after the other to the battery?
exp_2_1_v1: Both shine as brightly as one alone.
exp_2_1_b1: Both light up, but each dimmer than alone.
exp_2_1_s1: Put one bulb on A1–A2 and a second one on A2–A3.
exp_2_1_s2: Draw wires from +9V to A1 and from A3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_1_h1: The current flows through one bulb first, then the other.
exp_2_1_loesung: +9V → A1, bulb A1–A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V, battery 9 V.
exp_2_1_erklaerung: One after the other, the bulbs share the battery's voltage: each gets only half. That's why both are dimmer. This is called a series circuit.
exp_2_1_mehr: At 9 V each of the two 6 V bulbs gets about 4.5 V.
exp_2_1_w1: Turn on the voltage display at A2. How many bars do you see?
exp_2_1_w2: Take one bulb out. What happens to the other one?
exp_2_1_echt: Old fairy lights were series circuits: if one bulb broke, the whole string went dark.
exp_2_2_frage: This time each bulb gets its own path to the battery. Do they shine brighter than in a row?
exp_2_2_s1: Put one bulb on A1–A2 and one on B1–B2.
exp_2_2_s2: Connect A1 to B1 and A2 to B2.
exp_2_2_s3: Draw +9V to A1 and A2 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_2_h1: Each bulb should be connected directly to the battery at both ends.
exp_2_2_h2: Two cross wires connect the bulbs: A1–B1 and A2–B2.
exp_2_2_loesung: Bulbs A1–A2 and B1–B2, wires A1–B1, A2–B2, +9V → A1, A2 → 0V, battery 4.5 V.
exp_2_2_erklaerung: Side by side, each bulb gets the battery's full voltage. That's why both shine brightly. The battery has to deliver more current for it. This is called a parallel circuit.
exp_2_2_mehr: At home all lamps are connected in parallel – that's why each shines equally, however many are on.
exp_2_2_w1: Take one bulb out. Does the other keep shining?
exp_2_2_echt: Modern fairy lights are often wired in parallel. If one light fails, the others keep shining.
exp_2_3_frage: A machine should only run if panel switch S is on AND someone presses the button. How do you connect switch and button?
exp_2_3_b1: The bulb only lights when S is on and I press.
exp_2_3_s1: Put the button on A1–A2 and the bulb on A2–A3.
exp_2_3_s2: Draw +9V to S1, S2 to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp_2_3_s3: Try all four possibilities: S on/off, button pressed/not pressed.
exp_2_3_h1: The current should go through S first and then through the button.
exp_2_3_h2: If either is missing, the circuit is open.
exp_2_3_loesung: +9V → S1, S2 → A1, button A1–A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V. S on, press the button.
exp_2_3_erklaerung: When two switches lie one after the other, the current must pass through both. The bulb only lights if the first AND the second are closed. That's an AND circuit.
exp_2_3_mehr: Big machines have such safety features: they only run if two buttons are pressed at the same time.
exp_2_3_w1: Make a table: when does the bulb light and when not?
exp_2_3_echt: Some washing machines only start if the door is closed AND you press start.
exp_2_5_frage: A light should come on if panel switch S is on OR the button is pressed. How do you connect the two?
exp_2_5_b1: The bulb lights as soon as either one is closed.
exp_2_5_s1: Put the button on A1–A2 and the bulb on A2–A3.
exp_2_5_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and also +9V to S1, then S2 to A2.
exp_2_5_s3: Draw A3 to 0V. Try button and S one at a time.
exp_2_5_h1: The current should have two paths to the bulb.
exp_2_5_h2: S bridges the button: S1 to +9V, S2 to A2.
exp_2_5_loesung: +9V → A1 and +9V → S1, button A1–A2, S2 → A2, bulb A2–A3, A3 → 0V.
exp_2_5_erklaerung: When two switches lie side by side, the current has two paths. One open path is enough: the bulb lights if one OR the other is closed. That's an OR circuit.
exp_2_5_mehr: A car's interior light comes on if one OR the other door is open.
exp_2_5_w1: Compare with the AND circuit: what is wired differently?
exp_2_5_echt: A doorbell with two buttons, at the front and back of the house, is an OR circuit.
exp_2_6_frage: On a staircase you can switch the light on downstairs and off upstairs. How does that work with two switches?
exp_2_6_v1: With two changeover switches and two wires between them.
exp_2_6_v2: With two normal switches one after the other.
exp_2_6_b1: Each changeover switch can toggle the light, whatever the other's position.
exp_2_6_s1: Put one changeover switch on A1–A3, another on C1–C3 and the bulb on C5–C6.
exp_2_6_s2: Connect A1 to C1 and A3 to C3.
exp_2_6_s3: Draw +9V to A2, C2 to C5 and C6 to 0V. Tap the switches.
exp_2_6_h1: The middle of a changeover switch connects either to A or to B.
exp_2_6_h2: Two wires run between the switches: A to A and B to B.
exp_2_6_loesung: W1 on A1–A3, W2 on C1–C3, A1 → C1, A3 → C3, +9V → A2, C2 → C5, bulb C5–C6, C6 → 0V.
exp_2_6_erklaerung: The light is on when both changeover switches point to the same wire. If you flip one, they point to different wires and the path is broken. That way each switch can toggle the light.
exp_2_6_mehr: This circuit is called a two-way switching circuit. It's in almost every staircase and long hallway.
exp_2_6_w1: Try all four positions and note when the light is on.
exp_2_6_echt: Find a hallway at home or at school where you can switch the light at both ends.
exp_2_7_frage: A diode only lets current through in one direction. Does a bulb light if a diode sits in front of it?
exp_2_7_v1: Yes, if the diode is the right way round.
exp_2_7_b1: The right way round the bulb lights; the wrong way it stays dark.
exp_2_7_s1: Put the diode from B2 to B3 (ring towards B3) and a 10 V bulb on B3–B4.
exp_2_7_s2: Draw +9V to B2 and B4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_7_s3: Flip the diode (part menu: Flip). What happens?
exp_2_7_h1: The ring on the diode shows where the current may flow.
exp_2_7_h2: The ring belongs to the side that leads to 0V.
exp_2_7_loesung: +9V → B2, diode B2–B3 (ring at B3), 10 V bulb B3–B4, B4 → 0V.
exp_2_7_erklaerung: The diode is like a one-way street for current. In the forward direction it lets it through; in the reverse direction it stops it. That's why it matters which way round you put it.
exp_2_7_mehr: A diode uses up about 0.7 V. That's why you use a 10 V bulb here: it gets about 8.3 V.
exp_2_7_w1: Turn on the voltage display at B3 and flip the diode. What changes?
exp_2_7_echt: Diodes protect many devices: if you put the battery in the wrong way round, no current flows and nothing breaks.
exp_2_8_frage: An LED has a long and a short leg. Does it also light if you put it in the other way round?
exp_2_8_v1: No, only the right way round.
exp_2_8_b1: The other way round it stayed dark; the right way round it lights.
exp_2_8_s1: Put the resistor on B3–B4 and the LED from B4 to C4.
exp_2_8_s2: Draw +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_8_s3: Flip the LED until it lights.
exp_2_8_h1: An LED is a diode that lights – so it's a one-way street too.
exp_2_8_h2: The long leg (anode) belongs on the +9V side.
exp_2_8_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED long leg at B4, short leg at C4, C4 → 0V.
exp_2_8_erklaerung: An LED only lights in the forward direction. The long leg (anode) must go to plus, the short one (cathode) to minus. The wrong way round no current flows – but it doesn't break.
exp_2_8_mehr: The cathode side of the housing is often flattened.
exp_2_8_w1: Take a blue LED. Does it light with the same resistor?
exp_2_8_echt: Look at a real LED with an adult: can you find the long and the short leg?
exp_2_9_frage: A reed switch closes when a magnet is nearby. Can you build an alarm that buzzes when the magnet comes?
exp_2_9_v1: Yes, reed switch and buzzer one after the other.
exp_2_9_v2: I need a push button for that.
exp_2_9_b1: With the magnet it buzzes, without it it's quiet.
exp_2_9_s1: Put the reed switch on A1–A2 and the buzzer on A2–A3 (plus at A2).
exp_2_9_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_9_s3: Tap the reed switch – that holds the magnet next to it.
exp_2_9_h1: The reed switch is a switch operated by the magnet.
exp_2_9_h2: Reed switch and buzzer lie one after the other between +9V and 0V.
exp_2_9_loesung: +9V → A1, reed switch A1–A2, buzzer A2–A3, A3 → 0V. Bring the magnet close (tap).
exp_2_9_erklaerung: Inside the reed switch's glass tube are two thin metal tongues. A magnet pulls them together and the circuit closes. That's how a window or door can trigger an alarm.
exp_2_9_mehr: In real alarms the reed switch sits in the frame and the magnet in the window.
exp_2_9_w1: Build the alarm with a bulb instead of the buzzer. Which is easier to notice?
exp_2_9_echt: Some bike computers count wheel turns with a reed switch and a magnet on a spoke.
exp_2_10_frage: The blinker module switches on and off in rhythm. What happens if you connect the buzzer instead of a light?
exp_2_10_v2: The buzzer buzzes without a break.
exp_2_10_b1: The buzzer beeps briefly again and again.
exp_2_10_b2: The buzzer buzzes without a break.
exp_2_10_s1: Connect the blinker module: +9V to M1, M2 to 0V.
exp_2_10_s2: Put the buzzer on B2–B3 (plus at B2), draw +9V to B2.
exp_2_10_s3: Draw B3 to the module output (M3). Switch on.
exp_2_10_h1: Just like the blinking light – only with the buzzer.
exp_2_10_h2: The module output switches the path to 0V.
exp_2_10_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → B2, buzzer B2–B3, B3 → M3.
exp_2_10_erklaerung: The blinker module is like a button that presses and releases by itself. Whatever hangs on its output is switched in rhythm – a light blinks, a buzzer beeps.
exp_2_10_mehr: On the panel loudspeaker you can even see the pulses: its light ring blinks with every pulse.
exp_2_10_w1: Connect the panel loudspeaker (LS1/LS2) instead of the buzzer and watch the light ring.
exp_2_10_echt: Reversing beepers on lorries and alarm clocks beep in rhythm – there's a similar timing circuit behind them.
exp_2_11_frage: A traffic light for your bedroom door: with a changeover switch either red or green should light. Is that possible?
exp_2_11_v1: Yes, the changeover switch picks one of the two.
exp_2_11_b1: Depending on the position red or green lights, never both.
exp_2_11_s1: Put the changeover switch on A1–A3. Put the resistors from A1 to B1 and from A3 to B3 (vertical).
exp_2_11_s2: Put the red LED on B1–C1 and the green one on B3–C3, long leg at the top each.
exp_2_11_s3: Draw +9V to A2, C1 to 0V and C3 to C1. Switch to green.
exp_2_11_h1: Each LED needs its own series resistor.
exp_2_11_h2: The middle of the changeover switch gets +9V; A leads to red, B to green.
exp_2_11_loesung: W1 A1–A3, +9V → A2, R1 A1–B1, red LED B1–C1, R2 A3–B3, green LED B3–C3, C3 → C1 → 0V; switch to B (green).
exp_2_11_erklaerung: The changeover switch connects its middle to either one path or the other. That's why exactly one colour lights at a time: it chooses.
exp_2_11_mehr: Green LEDs need a bit more voltage than red ones, about 2.1 V instead of 1.9 V.
exp_2_11_w1: Add a yellow LED. Can you switch it on additionally with a push button?
exp_2_11_echt: Make a door traffic light out of paper: red means 'Do not disturb', green means 'Come in'.
exp_2_12_frage: You swap the 470 Ω resistor for a 1 kΩ one. Does the LED get brighter or dimmer?
exp_2_12_s1: Put a resistor on B3–B4 and set it to 1 kΩ (part menu: Value, or the toolbox).
exp_2_12_s2: Put the red LED on B4–C4, draw +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_12_h1: The colour bands for 1 kΩ are brown, black, red.
exp_2_12_h2: In the toolbox you can enter the value and apply it.
exp_2_12_loesung: 1 kΩ resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, +9V → B3, C4 → 0V.
exp_2_12_erklaerung: A bigger resistor slows the current down more. Less current flows through the LED and it shines less – but safely.
exp_2_12_mehr: With 1 kΩ about (9 V − 1.9 V) / 1000 Ω ≈ 7 mA flows instead of 15 mA.
exp_2_12_w1: Try 220 Ω, 470 Ω and 2.2 kΩ. Order them by brightness.
exp_2_12_echt: On many devices the power light is deliberately dim with a big resistor so it doesn't dazzle at night.
exp_1_8_titel: Light and fan with one switch
exp_1_8_frage: In the bathroom, one switch turns on the light and the fan at the same time. Can the panel switch S turn on a bulb and a motor together?
exp_1_8_v2: No, one switch can only handle one device.
exp_1_8_b1: The bulb and the motor go on and off together.
exp_1_8_s1: Put the bulb on B1–B2 and the motor on C1–C3.
exp_1_8_s2: Draw +9V to S1 and S2 to B1, then B1 to C1.
exp_1_8_s3: Draw B2 and C3 to 0V. Switch on and flip switch S.
exp_1_8_h1: Each device needs a path from the switch back to the battery.
exp_1_8_h2: Bulb and motor sit side by side: both starts at the switch, both ends at 0V.
exp_1_8_loesung: +9V → S1, S2 → B1, B1 → C1, bulb B1–B2, motor C1–C3, B2 → 0V, C3 → 0V.
exp_1_8_erklaerung: The switch sits before the branch. When it is on, both paths get current. Bulb and motor are connected in parallel: each one has its own path to the battery.
exp_1_8_mehr: If you take out the bulb, the motor keeps turning. In a parallel circuit every device works on its own.
exp_1_8_w1: What happens if you take out the bulb? Does the motor keep turning?
exp_1_8_echt: In many bathrooms the light switch also turns on the fan – both hang behind the same switch.
exp_1_9_frage: Someone who hears poorly hardly notices a doorbell. Can a single push button turn on the buzzer and a bulb at the same time?
exp_1_9_v2: No, then only the buzzer buzzes.
exp_1_9_b1: Buzzer and bulb respond together as long as I press.
exp_1_9_s1: Put the push button on A1–A2 and the buzzer on A2–A3 (plus at A2).
exp_1_9_s2: Put the bulb on B2–B3 and connect A2 to B2 and B3 to A3.
exp_1_9_s3: Draw +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V. Switch on and press the button.
exp_1_9_h1: The button goes at the start, before the branch.
exp_1_9_h2: After the button the path splits: one way through the buzzer, one through the bulb.
exp_1_9_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, buzzer A2–A3, A2 → B2, bulb B2–B3, B3 → A3, A3 → 0V.
exp_1_9_erklaerung: After the button the current splits into two paths. When you press, buzzer and bulb get current at the same time. When you let go, the path is broken for both.
exp_1_9_mehr: Light doorbells really exist. Often the light even flashes so that you notice it better.
exp_1_9_w1: Can you change the bell so that only the bulb comes on? What would you have to take out?
exp_1_9_echt: For people who hear poorly there are doorbells with a flashing light. Often the same button switches sound and light.
exp_1_10_frage: A bulb and a motor are connected one after the other to the battery. What does the bulb do when you hold the propeller still?
exp_1_10_b1: The bulb gets brighter when the propeller stops.
exp_1_10_s1: Put the bulb on A1–A2 and set it to 10 V (menu: rated voltage).
exp_1_10_s3: Draw +9V to A1 and A4 to 0V. Switch on. Then hold the propeller still.
exp_1_10_h1: Bulb and motor are in series: the current flows first through one, then through the other.
exp_1_10_h2: To hold the propeller, press and hold on the motor.
exp_1_10_loesung: +9V → A1, bulb A1–A2 (10 V), motor A2–A4, A4 → 0V.
exp_1_10_erklaerung: A turning motor acts like a small battery itself that pushes against the current. So little current flows and the bulb only glows faintly. If you hold the propeller, this push disappears: more current flows and the bulb shines brighter.
exp_1_10_mehr: That's why a blocked motor gets warm: much more current flows through its winding than while it is running.
exp_1_10_w1: Switch to the 6 V bulb. What happens now when you hold the propeller?
exp_1_10_echt: When a vacuum cleaner sounds strained, its motor draws more current. That's why many devices have a protection that switches off when blocked.
exp_2_13_titel: A song at the push of a button
exp_2_13_frage: Down in the module bar there is a tone module. It plays a little melody as long as its input "ein" gets current. Can you start it with a push button?
exp_2_13_v2: The melody always plays, even without pressing.
exp_2_13_b1: The melody plays as long as I press.
exp_2_13_b2: The melody plays without a break.
exp_2_13_s1: Power the tone module: +9V to + (M1) and − (M2) to 0V.
exp_2_13_s2: Draw +9V to LS1 and LS2 to the output "aus" (M4).
exp_2_13_s3: Put the push button on A1–A2, draw +9V to A1 and A2 to the input "ein" (M3). Switch on and press.
exp_2_13_h1: The module first needs current itself at + and −.
exp_2_13_h2: The button sits between +9V and the input "ein". The loudspeaker hangs between +9V and "aus".
exp_2_13_loesung: +9V → M1 (+), M2 (−) → 0V, +9V → LS1, LS2 → M4 (aus), +9V → A1, button A1–A2, A2 → M3 (ein).
exp_2_13_erklaerung: The input "ein" is like a start button for the module. When it gets voltage, the module plays its melody and its output stage switches the loudspeaker in time with the notes. Without voltage at the input it stays quiet.
exp_2_13_mehr: The loudspeaker's light ring shows the pitch as a colour: low notes more yellow, high ones orange to red. With "Look inside" you can see which note is playing.
exp_2_13_w1: Replace the push button with a wire. What happens now?
exp_2_13_echt: Musical greeting cards and toys with a tune have a similar chip – a small contact starts the melody.
exp_2_14_frage: Some shops play a tune when the door opens. Can a magnet at the reed switch start the tone module?
exp_2_14_v1: Yes, when the magnet comes, the tune plays.
exp_2_14_v2: No, you need a push button for that.
exp_2_14_b1: When the magnet comes, the tune plays. When it goes away, it's quiet.
exp_2_14_b2: The tune plays all the time.
exp_2_14_s1: Power the tone module (+9V to M1, M2 to 0V) and connect the loudspeaker (+9V to LS1, LS2 to M4).
exp_2_14_s2: Put the reed switch on A1–A2. Draw +9V to A1 and A2 to the input "ein" (M3).
exp_2_14_s3: Switch on and tap the reed switch – that's how the magnet comes.
exp_2_14_h1: The reed switch replaces the push button from the last experiment.
exp_2_14_h2: It closes as soon as the magnet is near.
exp_2_14_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → LS1, LS2 → M4, +9V → A1, reed switch A1–A2, A2 → M3.
exp_2_14_erklaerung: Inside the reed switch there are two thin metal reeds. A magnet pulls them together, and current flows to the input of the tone module. The module plays as long as the magnet is there.
exp_2_14_mehr: Instead of switching the input directly, you can also drive it through a resistor: the module responds from about 1.5 V.
exp_2_14_w1: Put a 10 kΩ resistor between the reed switch and the input. Does the tune still play?
exp_2_14_echt: Shop bells, alarm systems and fridge lights use such contacts – the magnet sits in the door, the contact in the frame.
exp_2_15_frage: The tone module plays too loud for you. Does the loudspeaker get quieter if a resistor sits in front of it?
exp_2_15_v1: Yes, with a resistor it gets quieter.
exp_2_15_b1: With the resistor the ring glows weaker: it's quieter.
exp_2_15_s1: Power the tone module (+9V to M1, M2 to 0V) and connect its input (M3) directly to +9V.
exp_2_15_s2: Put a 100 Ω resistor on A1–A2. Draw +9V to A1 and A2 to LS1.
exp_2_15_s3: Draw LS2 to M4 ("aus"). Switch on and watch the light ring.
exp_2_15_h1: The resistor belongs in the loudspeaker's path, between +9V and LS1.
exp_2_15_h2: Compare: once with the resistor, once with a wire instead.
exp_2_15_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → M3, +9V → A1, resistor 100 Ω A1–A2, A2 → LS1, LS2 → M4.
exp_2_15_erklaerung: The resistor slows down the current through the loudspeaker. Less current means the cone vibrates less strongly: the sound gets quieter. The light ring shows this as weaker light. The pitch stays the same – the module makes it.
exp_2_15_mehr: A bigger resistor makes the sound even quieter. A rotary control used as a resistor would be a volume control.
exp_2_15_w1: Try 220 Ω and 470 Ω. When can you hardly hear anything?
exp_2_15_echt: Older radios had a rotary knob for volume – it limited how much current flowed to the loudspeaker.
exp_2_16_frage: The blinker module has a pin called "Takt" (rate). Does the LED blink faster if you put a resistor from Takt to +9V?
exp_2_16_b1: With the resistor it blinks faster.
exp_2_16_s1: Build the blinker: +9V to M1, M2 to 0V, 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4, LED B4–C4, +9V to B3, C4 to M3 ("aus").
exp_2_16_s2: Put a 4.7 kΩ resistor on A1–A2.
exp_2_16_s3: Draw +9V to A1 and A2 to "Takt" (M4). Switch on and count the blinks.
exp_2_16_h1: First count, without the second resistor, how often the LED blinks in ten seconds.
exp_2_16_loesung: Blinker as in the start, plus +9V → A1, resistor 4.7 kΩ A1–A2, A2 → M4 (Takt).
exp_2_16_erklaerung: Inside the blinker module, capacitors charge through resistors. When they are charged, the circuit flips over. Your resistor at "Takt" is an extra path for the charging current: the capacitors charge faster and the module blinks faster.
exp_2_16_mehr: With "Look inside" you can see the capacitors C1 and C2. Their voltage rises and falls in time with the blinking.
exp_2_16_w1: Try 10 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ at "Takt". Which resistor makes it blink fastest?
exp_2_16_echt: Bike indicators and warning lights at road works have such timing circuits – one part decides how fast it blinks.
exp_2_17_frage: A vehicle reversing blinks and beeps at the same time. Can the blinker module switch an LED and the buzzer together in rhythm?
exp_2_17_v1: Yes, both in the same rhythm.
exp_2_17_v2: No, the module can only handle one.
exp_2_17_b1: LED and buzzer go on and off in the same rhythm.
exp_2_17_s1: Build the blinker: +9V to M1, M2 to 0V, 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4, LED B4–C4, +9V to B3, C4 to M3.
exp_2_17_s2: Put the buzzer on D2–D3 (plus at D2) and draw +9V to D2.
exp_2_17_s3: Draw D3 to the output M3 as well. Switch on.
exp_2_17_h1: Both devices hang with their end on the output "aus".
exp_2_17_h2: Seen from the output, LED and buzzer sit side by side.
exp_2_17_loesung: Blinker as in the start, plus +9V → D2, buzzer D2–D3, D3 → M3 (aus).
exp_2_17_erklaerung: The output of the blinker module opens and closes the path to 0V in rhythm. Everything connected to it is switched at the same time. That's why light and buzzer follow the same rhythm.
exp_2_17_mehr: With "Look inside" you can see that more current now flows through the output transistor T3 – it switches two devices.
exp_2_17_w1: Also connect the panel loudspeaker to the output (+9V to LS1, LS2 to M3). What does its light ring show?
exp_2_17_echt: Forklifts, street sweepers and lorries warn with light and sound at the same time when reversing.
exp_2_18_frage: With the rotary control P1 on the panel you can adjust a resistor. Can you use it to make the LED brighter and dimmer?
exp_2_18_v1: Yes, it gets brighter and dimmer.
exp_2_18_v2: No, it is only on or off.
exp_2_18_b1: Depending on the setting it shines brighter or dimmer.
exp_2_18_s1: Put the 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4 and the LED on B4–C4 (long leg at B4).
exp_2_18_s2: Draw +9V to B3 and C4 to P1a.
exp_2_18_s3: Draw P1s to 0V. Switch on and turn P1 until the LED only glows faintly.
exp_2_18_h1: The rotary control goes after the LED, between C4 and 0V.
exp_2_18_h2: Use the pins P1a and P1s. The wiper s slides along the resistance track.
exp_2_18_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, C4 → P1a, P1s → 0V; turn P1 roughly to the middle.
exp_2_18_erklaerung: Inside the rotary control a wiper slides over a resistance track. The further it is from P1a, the more track the current has to pass through: the resistance is bigger, the current smaller and the LED dimmer. The fixed resistor protects it even if you turn P1 all the way.
exp_2_18_mehr: The rotary control has 10 kΩ. In the middle that is about 5 kΩ – only a little over 1 mA flows and the LED just glows.
exp_2_18_w1: Can you dim without the fixed resistor? First think about what happens at the end stop.
exp_2_18_echt: Many lamps at home can be dimmed. Modern dimmers switch on and off very fast, but the idea "less current, less light" stays the same.
exp_2_19_frage: Is a single resistor enough for two LEDs if they sit one after the other?
exp_2_19_v2: No, only the first one lights up.
exp_2_19_b2: Only the red one lights up.
exp_2_19_s1: Put the 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4 and the red LED on B4–C4.
exp_2_19_s2: Put the green LED on C4–D4 (long leg at C4).
exp_2_19_s3: Draw +9V to B3 and D4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_19_h1: Both LEDs point the same way: long leg at the top.
exp_2_19_h2: The current flows one after the other through the resistor, the red and the green LED.
exp_2_19_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, red LED B4–C4, green LED C4–D4, D4 → 0V.
exp_2_19_erklaerung: In series the same current flows through all three parts. Each LED takes about 2 V, the rest of the 9 V drops across the resistor. So the current suits both.
exp_2_19_mehr: With three or four LEDs in series there is less and less voltage left for the resistor. At some point 9 V is no longer enough.
exp_2_19_w1: Add a third LED. How many can you light with 9 V?
exp_2_19_echt: In fairy lights and torches several LEDs often hang in series on one resistor.
exp_2_20_titel: Red or blue – who lights up?
exp_2_20_frage: A red and a blue LED sit side by side and share one resistor. Do both light up?
exp_2_20_b1: Only the red one lights up, the blue one stays dark.
exp_2_20_b3: Only the blue one lights up.
exp_2_20_s1: Put the 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4 and the red LED on B4–C4.
exp_2_20_s2: Put the blue LED on B4–B5 (long leg at B4).
exp_2_20_s3: Draw B5 to C4, +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_2_20_h1: Both LEDs start at B4 and end at 0V.
exp_2_20_h2: Check with the voltage display how much voltage there is at B4.
exp_2_20_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, red LED B4–C4, blue LED B4–B5, B5 → C4, C4 → 0V.
exp_2_20_erklaerung: A red LED starts to light at just under 2 V, a blue one needs about 3 V. Side by side both get the same voltage, and the red one holds it at 2 V. That's not enough for the blue one: all the current takes the easier path through the red one.
exp_2_20_mehr: That's why in circuits each LED gets its own resistor, especially with different colours.
exp_2_20_w1: Give the blue LED its own resistor. Do both light up now?
exp_2_20_echt: In devices with coloured indicators each LED has its own series resistor – otherwise only one colour would light up.
lex_heissleiter: A thermistor (NTC) conducts better when it gets warm: its resistance falls as the temperature rises.
lex_elektromagnet: A coil of wire on an iron core. When current flows it becomes a magnet – without current the magnet is off.
lex_relais: A relay is a switch worked by an electromagnet: a small current through the coil (A, B) closes the contact (COM, NO) for another circuit.
exp_3_1_titel: How much voltage does the battery have?
exp_3_1_frage: The panel says "9 V". Does the meter really show 9 volts when you connect it to the battery?
exp_3_1_s1: Show the meter (V A Ω) and set it to V.
exp_3_1_s2: Draw a red wire from +9V to the V/Ω socket.
exp_3_1_s3: Draw a black wire from COM to 0V. Switch on.
exp_3_1_h1: A voltmeter is connected at two points: plus and minus.
exp_3_1_h2: Red goes to V/Ω, black to COM.
exp_3_1_erklaerung: Voltage is the "push" with which the battery drives the current. The meter compares two points. Between plus and minus of the battery there are about 9 volts.
exp_3_1_mehr: If you set the battery to 4.5 V or 3 V on the panel, the meter shows the new value at once.
exp_3_1_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. What does the meter show?
exp_3_1_echt: Electricians use a meter to check whether a battery is still full. An empty 9 V battery often has only 7 V left.
exp_3_2_frage: Two identical bulbs are connected one after the other to 9 V. How much voltage does one of them get?
exp_3_2_s1: Put two bulbs on A1–A2 and A2–A3. Draw +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp_3_2_s2: Draw V/Ω to A1 and COM to A2: this measures across the first bulb.
exp_3_2_s3: Set the meter to V and switch on.
exp_3_2_h1: Measure across just one bulb: at its start and at its end.
exp_3_2_h2: The meter hangs next to the bulb, not in the row.
exp_3_2_loesung: Bulbs A1–A2 and A2–A3, +9V → A1, A3 → 0V, A1 → V/Ω, COM → A2.
exp_3_2_erklaerung: In series the bulbs share the battery voltage. Because they are identical, each gets about half. Together the two parts add up to 9 V again.
exp_3_2_mehr: Also measure across the second bulb and across both together. The parts add up to the whole voltage.
exp_3_2_w1: Measure across L2 (A2 and A3). Do L1 and L2 together make 9 V?
exp_3_2_echt: In old fairy lights many small bulbs hung in series on the mains; each got only a small part.
exp_3_3_titel: How much current flows through the LED?
exp_3_3_frage: To measure current, it has to flow through the meter. Where does the meter have to go?
exp_3_3_v1: Into the circuit, right in the middle.
exp_3_3_v2: Next to it, like when measuring voltage.
exp_3_3_b1: About 15 mA flows through the LED.
exp_3_3_s1: Put the 470 Ω resistor on B3–B4 and the LED on B4–C4. Draw +9V to B3.
exp_3_3_s2: Draw C4 to the A socket and COM to 0V: now the current has to go through the meter.
exp_3_3_s3: Set the meter to A and switch on.
exp_3_3_h1: To measure current, the meter replaces a piece of wire.
exp_3_3_h2: The path to 0V goes in through socket A and out at COM.
exp_3_3_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, C4 → A, COM → 0V, mode A.
exp_3_3_erklaerung: Current is the amount that flows round the circuit. For the meter to count it, the current has to pass through it: the meter goes into the circuit, not next to it. About 15 milliamps flow here, that is 0.015 A.
exp_3_3_mehr: An ammeter has almost no resistance inside. Connected straight to the battery a huge current would flow – that's why the meter has a fuse.
exp_3_3_w1: Use 1 kΩ instead of 470 Ω. How does the current change?
exp_3_3_echt: Electricians measure current to check whether a device draws too much – for example whether a bike light drains the battery too fast.
exp_3_4_titel: Does the current get used up on the way?
exp_3_4_frage: The LED lights up – does it use up current? Is the current bigger before the resistor than after it?
exp_3_4_v1: No, it is the same everywhere.
exp_3_4_v2: Yes, it is bigger at the start.
exp_3_4_b1: The same current flows at the start as at the end.
exp_3_4_b2: More current flows at the start.
exp_3_4_b3: Less current flows at the start.
exp_3_4_s1: Build resistor (B3–B4) and LED (B4–C4) as before, C4 to 0V.
exp_3_4_s2: Now put the meter at the start: +9V to A, COM to B3.
exp_3_4_s3: Set to A, switch on and compare with the last experiment.
exp_3_4_h1: This time the meter goes between battery and resistor.
exp_3_4_h2: Compare the value with the current at the end of the circuit.
exp_3_4_loesung: +9V → A, COM → B3, resistor B3–B4, LED B4–C4, C4 → 0V, mode A.
exp_3_4_erklaerung: Current is not used up. What flows into the circuit at the start comes out again at the end. What is used is energy: the LED turns it into light, the resistor into heat.
exp_3_4_mehr: Think of a bike chain: it moves at the same speed everywhere, but at the front you drive it and at the back it turns the wheel.
exp_3_4_w1: Also measure between resistor and LED (B4). What does the meter show?
exp_3_4_echt: The electricity meter at home doesn't measure current but energy – exactly what devices really use.
exp_3_5_frage: The resistor has rings: brown, black, red. That's supposed to mean 1000 Ω. Can you measure it?
exp_3_5_v1: Yes, the meter shows about 1000 Ω.
exp_3_5_s1: Put a resistor on A1–A2 and set it to 1 kΩ.
exp_3_5_s2: Draw A1 to V/Ω and COM to A2.
exp_3_5_s3: Set the meter to Ω. The main switch can stay off.
exp_3_5_h1: When measuring resistance the meter sends a small current through by itself.
exp_3_5_h2: The resistor must not be in a circuit with a battery.
exp_3_5_loesung: Resistor 1 kΩ A1–A2, A1 → V/Ω, COM → A2, mode Ω.
exp_3_5_erklaerung: In the ohm range the meter has its own small battery. It sends current through the resistor and works out how strongly it slows it down. Colour code and measurement agree.
exp_3_5_mehr: In the toolbox you'll find the colour code table. With it you can read every resistor and then measure it.
exp_3_5_w1: Set the resistor to 470 Ω. What colours does it have now, and what do you measure?
exp_3_5_echt: In the electronics workshop resistors are checked by measuring, because colours can be hard to tell apart – red and orange, for example.
exp_3_6_frage: 9 volts drive current through a 1000 Ω resistor. How much current flows?
exp_3_6_s1: Put a 1 kΩ resistor on B3–B4 and draw +9V to B3.
exp_3_6_s2: Draw B4 to the A socket and COM to 0V.
exp_3_6_s3: Set to A and switch on.
exp_3_6_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor 1 kΩ B3–B4, B4 → A, COM → 0V, mode A.
exp_3_6_erklaerung: The higher the voltage, the more current; the bigger the resistance, the less. That is Ohm's law: current = voltage ÷ resistance. Here: 9 V ÷ 1000 Ω = 9 mA.
exp_3_6_mehr: It is named after Georg Simon Ohm. About 200 years ago he discovered that current and voltage rise together.
exp_3_6_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Does the current halve?
exp_3_6_echt: With this formula engineers work out which resistor an LED needs – now you can do that too.
exp_3_7_frage: You need 3 V, but the battery has 9 V. Can rotary control P1 tap off a smaller voltage?
exp_3_7_v1: Yes, with the rotary control I set 3 V.
exp_3_7_v2: No, the battery always has 9 V.
exp_3_7_b1: At the wiper I can set any voltage between 0 and 9 V.
exp_3_7_s1: Draw +9V to P1a and P1b to 0V: the whole voltage is across the rotary control.
exp_3_7_s2: Draw the wiper P1s to V/Ω and COM to 0V. Set to V.
exp_3_7_s3: Switch on and turn P1 until the meter shows 3 V.
exp_3_7_h1: The rotary control is a long resistor with a tap that slides along it.
exp_3_7_h2: The closer the wiper is to +9V, the higher the voltage.
exp_3_7_loesung: +9V → P1a, P1b → 0V, P1s → V/Ω, COM → 0V; P1 about one third from the bottom.
exp_3_7_erklaerung: The rotary control divides the battery voltage into two parts. The wiper picks off the voltage somewhere in between. So any smaller voltage can be made from 9 V – a voltage divider.
exp_3_7_mehr: Two fixed resistors in series also divide the voltage: two equal ones exactly in the middle.
exp_3_7_w1: Build a divider from two 1 kΩ resistors. What do you measure in the middle?
exp_3_7_echt: Volume knobs on old radios were exactly such a rotary control: they passed on only part of the sound signal.
exp_3_8_frage: The room is dark. Does the LED shine brighter when the torch shines on the photoresistor?
exp_3_8_v1: Yes, with light it gets brighter.
exp_3_8_b1: With light the LED shines brightly, in the dark hardly at all.
exp_3_8_s1: Put the photoresistor on A1–A3 (long), the 470 Ω resistor on A3–A4 and the LED on A4–B4.
exp_3_8_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and B4 to 0V. Switch on.
exp_3_8_s3: Put the torch on the photoresistor (bar at the bottom left) and switch it on and off.
exp_3_8_h1: Light and heat are in the bar at the bottom left.
exp_3_8_h2: The closer the torch is to the photoresistor, the more light it gets.
exp_3_8_loesung: +9V → A1, photoresistor A1–A3, resistor A3–A4, LED A4–B4, B4 → 0V; torch on A2.
exp_3_8_erklaerung: Inside the photoresistor is a material that lets more current through in light. In the dark its resistance is very large, in light it is small. That's why the light controls the current.
exp_3_8_mehr: A photoresistor reacts a little slowly: it needs a moment to adjust to new light.
exp_3_8_w1: Slowly move the torch away. How does the LED change?
exp_3_8_echt: Street lamps and night lights have a light sensor: when it gets dark they switch on.
exp_3_9_titel: How big is the resistance in the dark?
exp_3_9_frage: You measure the photoresistor with the meter. Does its resistance get bigger or smaller when it gets dark?
exp_3_9_b1: In the dark it measures many kilo-ohms, in light only a few hundred ohms.
exp_3_9_b3: In the dark it is smaller.
exp_3_9_s1: Put the photoresistor on A1–A3 (long). Draw A1 to V/Ω and COM to A3.
exp_3_9_s3: Switch the room light between bright, twilight and dark and read the value each time.
exp_3_9_h1: You change the room light in the bar at the bottom left.
exp_3_9_h2: Watch the unit: kΩ means a thousand ohms.
exp_3_9_loesung: Photoresistor A1–A3, A1 → V/Ω, COM → A3, mode Ω, room light dark.
exp_3_9_erklaerung: In the dark the photoresistor has hardly any free charges to carry the current – its resistance is large. Light creates new free charges, and the resistance drops sharply.
exp_3_9_mehr: From bright room light to darkness the resistance changes a hundredfold.
exp_3_9_w1: Put the torch right on top. How small does the resistance get?
exp_3_9_echt: Cameras measure how bright it is with light sensors and set the exposure accordingly.
exp_3_10_frage: A thermistor sits in front of the LED. What happens when the hair dryer warms it up?
exp_3_10_b1: With warm air the LED slowly gets brighter.
exp_3_10_s1: Put the thermistor on C1–C3 (long) and the LED on C3–D3.
exp_3_10_s2: Draw +9V to C1 and D3 to 0V. Switch on: the LED only glows faintly.
exp_3_10_s3: Put the hair dryer on the thermistor (bar at the bottom left) and wait a few seconds.
exp_3_10_h1: The thermistor needs a few seconds to warm up.
exp_3_10_h2: Watch the temperature on its label.
exp_3_10_loesung: +9V → C1, thermistor C1–C3, LED C3–D3, D3 → 0V; hair dryer on C2.
exp_3_10_erklaerung: A thermistor conducts better the warmer it is: its resistance falls with temperature. So more current flows and the LED gets brighter. If you switch the dryer off, it cools down and the LED gets dimmer again.
exp_3_10_mehr: At 20 °C this thermistor has about 12 kΩ, at 80 °C only about 1.3 kΩ.
exp_3_10_w1: Switch the dryer off. How long does it take for the LED to get dim again?
exp_3_10_echt: Thermistors measure the temperature in fever thermometers, fridges and heating systems.
exp_3_11_titel: A thermometer made from a resistor
exp_3_11_frage: You measure the thermistor's resistance. What does the meter show when the hair dryer blows?
exp_3_11_b1: The resistance falls the warmer it gets.
exp_3_11_s1: Put the thermistor on C1–C3 (long). Draw C1 to V/Ω and COM to C3.
exp_3_11_s2: Set the meter to Ω and read the value at room temperature.
exp_3_11_s3: Put the hair dryer on it and watch the meter.
exp_3_11_h1: Without the dryer it's over 10 kΩ.
exp_3_11_h2: With the dryer the value drops below 5 kΩ.
exp_3_11_loesung: Thermistor C1–C3, C1 → V/Ω, COM → C3, mode Ω; hair dryer on C2.
exp_3_11_erklaerung: Each temperature belongs to a certain resistance. Whoever measures the resistance knows the temperature. That turns the thermistor into a thermometer.
exp_3_11_mehr: With the recorder and the meter you can record the cooling curve.
exp_3_11_w1: Record how the resistance rises again after switching off the dryer.
exp_3_11_echt: Digital thermometers contain a thermistor and convert the measured resistance into degrees.
exp_3_12_frage: An electrolytic capacitor is connected to the battery through a resistor. Is it fully charged at once?
exp_3_12_b1: The voltage rises fast at first, then more and more slowly to almost 9 V.
exp_3_12_b2: The voltage is 9 V at once.
exp_3_12_s1: Put the 10 kΩ resistor on B3–B4 and the capacitor on B4–C4 (plus at B4). Draw +9V to B3 and C4 to 0V.
exp_3_12_s2: Open the recorder (📈) and connect channel 1 to B4: long press on B4.
exp_3_12_s3: Switch on and watch the curve.
exp_3_12_h1: The recorder draws the voltage across the capacitor.
exp_3_12_h2: The resistor slows down the charging current.
exp_3_12_loesung: +9V → B3, resistor 10 kΩ B3–B4, capacitor B4–C4, C4 → 0V; recorder channel 1 at B4.
exp_3_12_erklaerung: The capacitor collects charge like a container fills with water. At first a lot flows in, the fuller it gets, the slower. That's why the curve rises steeply first and then flattens.
exp_3_12_mehr: Resistance times capacitance gives the time constant: 10 kΩ × 100 µF = 1 second. After about 5 time constants the capacitor is practically full.
exp_3_12_w1: Use 1 kΩ instead of 10 kΩ. How fast is the capacitor full now?
exp_3_12_echt: In a camera flash a capacitor charges slowly and then releases its charge in a flash.
exp_3_13_frage: A big capacitor sits next to the LED. What happens when you let go of the button?
exp_3_13_v1: The LED keeps shining for a while.
exp_3_13_b1: It keeps glowing and slowly gets dimmer.
exp_3_13_s1: Put the push button on A1–A2 and the capacitor (1000 µF) on A2–A3, plus at A2. Draw +9V to A1 and A3 to 0V.
exp_3_13_s2: Draw A2 to B2. Put the 1 kΩ resistor on B2–B3 and the LED on B3–C3, C3 to 0V.
exp_3_13_s3: Switch on, press the button briefly and let go.
exp_3_13_h1: While you press, the capacitor charges.
exp_3_13_h2: After letting go, the capacitor gives its charge to the LED.
exp_3_13_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, capacitor A2–A3 (1000 µF), A3 → 0V, A2 → B2, resistor B2–B3, LED B3–C3, C3 → 0V.
exp_3_13_erklaerung: The capacitor is like a small store. When you press, it fills up; when you let go, it takes over the role of the battery. The emptier it gets, the dimmer the LED.
exp_3_13_mehr: With the recorder at A2 you see the discharge curve: it falls fast first, then more and more slowly.
exp_3_13_w1: Use 10 kΩ instead of 1 kΩ. Does the LED keep glowing longer or shorter?
exp_3_13_echt: Some devices have a capacitor so that the clock keeps running while you change the battery.
exp_3_14_titel: A magnet you can switch on
exp_3_14_frage: A coil of wire on an iron core. Does it become a magnet when current flows through it?
exp_3_14_v1: Yes, it attracts the paper clip.
exp_3_14_b1: With current it attracts the paper clip, without current it lets go.
exp_3_14_s1: Put the push button on A1–A2 and the electromagnet on A2–A4 (long).
exp_3_14_s2: Draw +9V to A1 and A4 to 0V.
exp_3_14_s3: Switch on and press the button.
exp_3_14_h1: The current has to flow through the coil.
exp_3_14_h2: Watch the paper clip at the electromagnet.
exp_3_14_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, electromagnet A2–A4, A4 → 0V.
exp_3_14_erklaerung: Current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field. Many turns on an iron core make it strong. Without current the field disappears – a magnet you can switch on and off.
exp_3_14_mehr: The more current flows, the stronger the magnet. At 3 V it pulls more weakly than at 9 V.
exp_3_14_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. Does the magnet still hold the paper clip?
exp_3_14_echt: Scrapyards lift cars with huge electromagnets. Electromagnets are also inside door openers and loudspeakers.
exp_3_15_titel: A switch that switches by itself
exp_3_15_frage: The push button sends current only through the relay's coil. Does the bulb, which is in another circuit, still come on?
exp_3_15_v1: Yes, the relay switches the bulb.
exp_3_15_v2: No, the bulb gets no current from the button.
exp_3_15_b1: When I press, the relay clicks and the bulb lights up.
exp_3_15_s1: Put the relay on C3 (A, B at the top; COM, NO at the bottom). Put the button on A3–B3, draw +9V to A3, B3 to C3 and C4 to 0V.
exp_3_15_s2: Draw +9V to D3 (COM). Draw D4 (NO) to E4.
exp_3_15_s3: Put the bulb on E4–E5 and set it to 10 V, E5 to 0V. Switch on and press the button.
exp_3_15_h1: The relay has two circuits: the coil (A, B) and the contact (COM, NO).
exp_3_15_h2: The button controls only the coil. The contact switches the bulb.
exp_3_15_loesung: +9V → A3, button A3–B3, B3 → C3, relay C3/C4/D3/D4, C4 → 0V, +9V → D3, D4 → E4, bulb E4–E5 (10 V), E5 → 0V.
exp_3_15_erklaerung: Inside the relay is an electromagnet. When current flows through its coil, it pulls a metal reed and the contact closes. So a small current controls a completely different circuit.
exp_3_15_mehr: The relay needs about 30 mA to pull in and only lets go below about 12 mA. This difference stops it from chattering.
exp_3_15_w1: Connect the motor to the contact instead of the bulb. Does that work too?
exp_3_15_echt: In cars, relays switch the headlights and the starter: the switch at the steering wheel only controls a small current.
lex_feuchtesonde: Two bare contacts: dry, no current flows; water between them conducts a little.
lex_piezo: A piezo sounder beeps high and needs very little current. Plus and minus must be right.
lex_zeitmodul: The timer module switches its output on for a few seconds after a short press on "start".
lex_verstaerkermodul: The amplifier module turns a tiny current at its input into a large one at its output.
exp_4_1_frage: The push button sends only a tiny current into the base of the transistor. Can the transistor switch on the LED with that?
exp_4_1_v1: Yes, the transistor switches it on.
exp_4_1_v2: No, the current is far too small.
exp_4_1_b1: When I press, the LED lights brightly.
exp_4_1_s1: Put the transistor on C3 (B and C at the top, E at the bottom). Draw D3 (E) to 0V.
exp_4_1_s2: Push button on A3–B3, +9V to A3; 10 kΩ resistor on B3–C3 to the base.
exp_4_1_s3: 470 Ω resistor on A5–B5 with +9V at A5, LED B5–C5, C5 to C4 (C). Switch on and press.
exp_4_1_h1: The small circuit: +9V, button, 10 kΩ, base, emitter, 0V.
exp_4_1_h2: The big circuit: +9V, 470 Ω, LED, collector, emitter, 0V.
exp_4_1_loesung: +9V → A3, button A3–B3, 10 kΩ B3–C3, transistor C3/C4/D3/D4, D3 → 0V, +9V → A5, 470 Ω A5–B5, LED B5–C5, C5 → C4.
exp_4_1_erklaerung: A transistor has three legs. When a small current flows into the base, it opens the path from collector to emitter for a much larger current. Without base current it blocks. So a small current switches a big one – with no moving parts.
exp_4_1_mehr: Less than 1 mA flows into the base through the 10 kΩ resistor, about 15 mA through the LED.
exp_4_1_w1: Replace the button with the moisture probe. Is a drop of water enough?
exp_4_1_echt: Every computer and phone contains billions of tiny transistors working as switches.
exp_4_2_titel: How much does a transistor amplify?
exp_4_2_frage: Only about 0.08 mA flows into the base. How big does the collector current get?
exp_4_2_v2: Much more – about 200 times as much.
exp_4_2_b1: About 16 mA flows at the collector – roughly 200 times more.
exp_4_2_b2: Just as little flows as into the base.
exp_4_2_s1: 100 kΩ resistor on B2–B3, +9V to B2. Transistor on B3 (B top left), C3 (E) to 0V.
exp_4_2_s2: 220 Ω resistor on A5–A6, +9V to A5. A6 to socket A, COM to the collector B4.
exp_4_2_s3: Meter on A, switch on, read the value.
exp_4_2_h1: Base current: (9 V − 0.7 V) ÷ 100 kΩ ≈ 0.08 mA.
exp_4_2_h2: The meter sits in the collector circuit.
exp_4_2_loesung: +9V → B2, 100 kΩ B2–B3, transistor B3/B4/C3/C4, C3 → 0V, +9V → A5, 220 Ω A5–A6, A6 → A, COM → B4, mode A.
exp_4_2_erklaerung: The transistor amplifies: the collector current is a fixed multiple of the base current – for this transistor about 200 times. This number is called the current gain.
exp_4_2_mehr: The gain only holds as long as the collector circuit allows enough current. With a big resistor at the collector the transistor is fully on – then it works as a switch.
exp_4_2_w1: Use 47 kΩ at the base. Does the collector current roughly double?
exp_4_2_echt: In hearing aids and microphone amplifiers transistors turn tiny currents into big ones.
exp_4_3_titel: A night light that switches itself on
exp_4_3_frage: A photoresistor and a transistor: can the LED come on by itself when it gets dark?
exp_4_3_v1: Yes, in the dark it comes on.
exp_4_3_v2: No, it comes on in light.
exp_4_3_b1: In the dark it lights up, in light it is off.
exp_4_3_s1: 47 kΩ resistor on B1–B2 (+9V at B1), photoresistor on B2–C2, C2 to 0V.
exp_4_3_s2: Transistor on B4, E (C4) to 0V. Draw B2 to the base B4.
exp_4_3_s3: 470 Ω resistor A6–A7 (+9V at A6), LED A7–B7, B7 to the collector B5. Change the room light.
exp_4_3_h1: In light the photoresistor pulls the base towards 0V.
exp_4_3_h2: In the dark the photoresistor gets big – the base gets current through the 47 kΩ.
exp_4_3_loesung: +9V → B1, 47 kΩ B1–B2, photoresistor B2–C2, C2 → 0V, B2 → B4, transistor B4/B5/C4/C5, C4 → 0V, +9V → A6, 470 Ω A6–A7, LED A7–B7, B7 → B5.
exp_4_3_erklaerung: Resistor and photoresistor divide the voltage. In light the photoresistor is small and less than 0.6 V is left at the base – the transistor blocks. In the dark it gets big, the base voltage rises and the transistor switches the LED on.
exp_4_3_mehr: At twilight the LED already glows a little: the transistor is half open.
exp_4_3_w1: Swap the photoresistor and the 47 kΩ resistor. What happens in light now?
exp_4_3_echt: Street lamps and garden lights switch on with exactly this kind of twilight switch.
exp_4_4_frage: This time the photoresistor is at the top, at +9V. What does the LED do when the torch shines on it?
exp_4_4_b1: With the torch it lights up, without it stays dark.
exp_4_4_b2: It only lights in the dark.
exp_4_4_s1: Photoresistor long on B1–B3 (+9V at B1), 4.7 kΩ resistor on B3–C3, C3 to 0V.
exp_4_4_s2: Transistor on B5, E (C5) to 0V, B3 to the base B5.
exp_4_4_s3: 470 Ω on A7–A8 (+9V at A7), green LED A8–B8, B8 to the collector B6. Room dark, torch on the photoresistor.
exp_4_4_h1: Photoresistor at the top, fixed resistor at the bottom – the other way round from the night light.
exp_4_4_h2: Light makes the photoresistor small, the base gets voltage.
exp_4_4_loesung: +9V → B1, photoresistor B1–B3, 4.7 kΩ B3–C3, C3 → 0V, B3 → B5, transistor B5/B6/C5/C6, C5 → 0V, +9V → A7, 470 Ω A7–A8, LED A8–B8, B8 → B6.
exp_4_4_erklaerung: The voltage divider is turned round: in light the top photoresistor gets small, the base gets plenty of voltage and the transistor switches on. In the dark it blocks.
exp_4_4_mehr: A light barrier works the other way round: when the beam is interrupted, it switches.
exp_4_4_w1: Slowly move the torch away. At what distance does the LED go off?
exp_4_4_echt: Light barriers open lift doors, count visitors and secure garage doors.
exp_4_5_frage: The thermistor sits at the top of the divider. Does the piezo beep when the hair dryer warms the thermistor?
exp_4_5_v2: No, it only beeps when cold.
exp_4_5_b1: Cold it is quiet, warm the piezo beeps.
exp_4_5_s1: Thermistor long on B1–B3 (+9V at B1), 680 Ω resistor on B3–C3, C3 to 0V.
exp_4_5_s2: Transistor on B5, E (C5) to 0V, B3 to the base B5.
exp_4_5_s3: Piezo on A6–B6 (plus at A6, +9V at A6), minus at the collector B6. Put the hair dryer on the thermistor.

exp_4_5_h2: Cold, the thermistor stays big and the transistor blocks.
exp_4_5_loesung: +9V → B1, thermistor B1–B3, 680 Ω B3–C3, C3 → 0V, B3 → B5, transistor B5/B6/C5/C6, C5 → 0V, +9V → A6, piezo A6–B6.
exp_4_5_erklaerung: At room temperature the thermistor has over 10 kΩ and the base gets only about 0.5 V – too little. When it gets warm its resistance falls, the base voltage rises above 0.6 V and the transistor switches the piezo on.
exp_4_5_mehr: With a different fixed resistor you set the temperature at which the alarm goes off.
exp_4_5_w1: Use 470 Ω instead of 680 Ω. Does the alarm now need more or less heat?
exp_4_5_echt: Fire detectors and overheating protection in devices work with temperature sensors.
exp_4_6_frage: Water conducts only a little. Is this small current enough for the transistor to switch on the piezo?
exp_4_6_b1: When the probe is wet, the piezo beeps.
exp_4_6_s1: Moisture probe long on B1–B3, +9V at B1.
exp_4_6_s2: Transistor on B4, E (C4) to 0V. The probe ends at the base B4 (B3 to B4).

exp_4_6_h1: The probe replaces the base resistor.
exp_4_6_h2: Wet probe: a few tenths of a milliamp flow into the base.
exp_4_6_loesung: +9V → B1, moisture probe B1–B3, B3 → B4, transistor B4/B5/C4/C5, C4 → 0V, +9V → A5, piezo A5–B5.
exp_4_6_erklaerung: Dry, the probe is practically open. A drop of water connects its contacts and a small current flows into the base. The transistor amplifies it enough for the piezo to beep.
exp_4_6_mehr: Pure water hardly conducts; tap water conducts because of the dissolved salts in it.
exp_4_6_w1: Put the drop one field next to the probe. Does it still beep?
exp_4_6_echt: Water alarms under the washing machine warn you before the cellar gets flooded.
exp_4_7_titel: Just a little moisture is enough
exp_4_7_frage: The water drop is only at the edge of the probe, it is hardly damp. Does the amplifier module still notice something?
exp_4_7_b1: The piezo beeps although the probe is hardly wet.
exp_4_7_b3: It beeps even when completely dry.

exp_4_7_s2: Moisture probe long on A1–A3, +9V at A1, A3 to the input "ein" (M3).
exp_4_7_s3: Piezo on B5–C5, +9V at B5, C5 to the output "aus" (M4). Water drop on A3.
exp_4_7_h1: The module contains two transistors one after the other.
exp_4_7_h2: A few millionths of an amp at the input are enough.

exp_4_7_erklaerung: In the amplifier module one transistor amplifies the current and a second one amplifies it again – together about 40,000 times. That's why a hardly damp probe is enough.
exp_4_7_mehr: With "Look inside" you can see which of the two transistors conducts.
exp_4_7_w1: Build the alarm from the last experiment with just one transistor and put the drop next to the probe too. What's different?
exp_4_7_echt: Rain sensors on car windscreens and soil moisture meters for plants are similarly sensitive.
exp_4_8_frage: One short press on the button – does the light stay on for a while afterwards?
exp_4_8_v1: Yes, it stays on for a few seconds.
exp_4_8_v2: No, it goes off at once.
exp_4_8_b1: The light stays on for about 3 seconds and then goes off.
exp_4_8_s1: Power the timer module: +9V to M1 (+), M2 (−) to 0V.
exp_4_8_s2: Push button on A1–A2, +9V at A1, A2 to the input "start" (M3).
exp_4_8_s3: 470 Ω resistor B3–B4 (+9V at B3), LED B4–C4, C4 to the output "aus" (M4). Press briefly.
exp_4_8_h1: The button only gives the kick.
exp_4_8_h2: The timer module then keeps its output on by itself.

exp_4_8_mehr: With "Look inside" you can see the capacitor voltage moving and the transistors switching.
exp_4_8_w1: Hold the button down longer. How long does the light stay on now?
exp_4_8_echt: Stairwell lights, escalators and hand dryers switch off by themselves after a while.
exp_4_9_frage: A capacitor stores charge, a transistor switches. Can they make a light that keeps shining after you let go?
exp_4_9_v1: Yes, it keeps shining for a while.
exp_4_9_v2: No, it goes off at once.
exp_4_9_b1: After letting go it stays bright for a few seconds and then goes off.
exp_4_9_b3: It only fades slowly like with the capacitor alone.
exp_4_9_s1: Button A1–A2 (+9V at A1), capacitor 1000 µF A2–A3 (plus at A2), A3 to 0V.
exp_4_9_s2: A2 to B2, 10 kΩ resistor B2–B3, transistor on B3, E (C3) to 0V.
exp_4_9_s3: 470 Ω A5–A6 (+9V at A5), LED A6–B6, B6 to the collector B4. Press and let go.
exp_4_9_h1: The capacitor feeds the base when the button is open.
exp_4_9_h2: The base current is tiny – that's why the charge lasts long.
exp_4_9_loesung: +9V → A1, button A1–A2, capacitor A2–A3, A3 → 0V, A2 → B2, 10 kΩ B2–B3, transistor B3/B4/C3/C4, C3 → 0V, +9V → A5, 470 Ω A5–A6, LED A6–B6, B6 → B4.
exp_4_9_erklaerung: The capacitor discharges only through the base – and the transistor needs little current for that. So the charge lasts much longer than in experiment 3.13, and the LED stays bright until the capacitor is almost empty. The timer module is built like this too.
exp_4_9_mehr: The time depends on capacitor and resistor: bigger resistor, longer time.
exp_4_9_w1: Use 47 kΩ instead of 10 kΩ. How long does the light stay on now?
exp_4_9_echt: The interior light in a car stays on after you close the door – often with exactly this kind of circuit.
exp_4_10_titel: A flip-flop flasher from single parts
exp_4_10_frage: Two transistors, two capacitors, two LEDs – cross-connected. Do the LEDs blink in turn?
exp_4_10_v2: No, both shine all the time.
exp_4_10_b1: Red and green blink in turn.
exp_4_10_s1: Left: 470 Ω A2–A3 (+9V at A2), red LED A3–B3; 10 kΩ B1–B2 (+9V at B1); transistor T1 on B2, C2 to 0V.
exp_4_10_s2: Right: 470 Ω A8–A9 (+9V at A9), green LED A8–B8; 10 kΩ B6–B7 (+9V at B6); transistor T2 on B7, C7 to 0V.
exp_4_10_s3: Crosswise: capacitor C1 D3–D4 (B3 to D3, D4 to the base B7); capacitor C2 E8–E7 (B8 to E8, E7 to the base B2). Switch on.
exp_4_10_h1: Each collector is connected through a capacitor to the base of the other transistor.
exp_4_10_h2: Watch the capacitor polarity: plus to the collector.
exp_4_10_loesung: Two transistor stages (B2, B7) with LEDs at the collector; capacitor from collector T1 to base T2 and from collector T2 to base T1.
exp_4_10_erklaerung: When one transistor switches on, its collector voltage jumps down. The capacitor passes this jump to the base of the other, which blocks – until the capacitor has recharged through 10 kΩ. Then everything flips the other way. That's exactly how the blinker module works inside.
exp_4_10_mehr: Compare with the "Look inside" view of the blinker module: you have built the same circuit yourself.
exp_4_10_w1: Use 47 kΩ instead of 10 kΩ at one base. What changes in the rhythm?
exp_4_10_echt: Level crossings and road works warn with alternating flashers.
exp_4_11_frage: The magnet sits on the door, the reed switch on the frame. As long as the door is shut, the contact is closed. Does the alarm go off when the door opens?
exp_4_11_v1: Yes, when it opens the tune plays.
exp_4_11_v2: No, it only plays with the door shut.
exp_4_11_b1: Door shut: quiet. Door open: the tune plays.
exp_4_11_s1: Power the tone module (+9V to M1, M2 to 0V) and connect the loudspeaker (+9V to LS1, LS2 to M4).
exp_4_11_s2: 10 kΩ resistor A1–A2 (+9V at A1), A2 to the input "ein" (M3).
exp_4_11_s3: Reed switch A2–A3, A3 to 0V. Tap the reed switch: magnet there (door shut) or away (door open).
exp_4_11_h1: The reed switch pulls the input to 0V as long as it is closed.
exp_4_11_h2: When it opens, the resistor pulls the input to +9V.
exp_4_11_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → LS1, LS2 → M4, +9V → A1, 10 kΩ A1–A2, A2 → M3, reed switch A2–A3, A3 → 0V.
exp_4_11_erklaerung: The reed switch holds the tone module's input at 0 V as long as the magnet is there. When the door opens, the contact opens and the resistor brings the input to +9V – the tone module plays.
exp_4_11_mehr: This is called a closed-circuit alarm: even if someone cuts the wire, the alarm goes off.
exp_4_11_w1: Replace the loudspeaker with the LED and its resistor. Is that still a good alarm?
exp_4_11_echt: Alarm systems on windows and doors use magnetic contacts like this one.
exp_4_12_frage: The relay's contact also feeds its own coil. What happens when you press the button briefly and let go?
exp_4_12_b1: Pressed once, the bulb stays on – until the power is switched off.
exp_4_12_b2: It goes off after letting go.
exp_4_12_b3: It doesn't come on at all.
exp_4_12_s1: Relay on C3, C4 (B) to 0V. Button A3–B3, +9V at A3, B3 to the coil C3.
exp_4_12_s2: +9V to COM (D3). Draw NO (D4) back to the coil C3.
exp_4_12_s3: Also draw D4 to E4, bulb E4–E5 (10 V), E5 to 0V. Press briefly.
exp_4_12_h1: The wire from NO back to the coil is the trick.
exp_4_12_h2: Once the relay has pulled in, its coil gets current through its own contact.
exp_4_12_loesung: +9V → A3, button A3–B3, B3 → C3, C4 → 0V, +9V → D3, D4 → C3, D4 → E4, bulb E4–E5, E5 → 0V.
exp_4_12_erklaerung: The button only gives the first push. As soon as the relay has pulled in, its own contact feeds the coil – it holds itself. It only drops out when the power is switched off. Such a circuit remembers something: a memory.
exp_4_12_mehr: With a second button that interrupts the current you get an on-off switch with two buttons.
exp_4_12_w1: Switch the main switch off and on again. Is the bulb on or off afterwards?
exp_4_12_echt: Big machines have a green start button and a red stop button – behind them is a self-holding circuit.
exp_4_13_frage: One transistor amplifies 200 times. What happens when a second one amplifies the amplified current again?
exp_4_13_v1: The circuit gets much more sensitive.
exp_4_13_b1: Even a hardly damp probe makes the piezo beep.
exp_4_13_b2: It needs a completely wet probe.
exp_4_13_s1: Moisture probe long on A1–A3, +9V at A1, A3 to the base of T1 (B5). 1 MΩ resistor on A3–A4, A4 to 0V. Collector T1 (B6) to +9V.
exp_4_13_s2: Emitter T1 (C5) to the base of T2 (B9). Emitter T2 (C9) to 0V.
exp_4_13_s3: Piezo on A10–B10, +9V at A10 – minus at the collector of T2 (B10). Water drop on A3.
exp_4_13_h1: The emitter current of T1 is the base current of T2.
exp_4_13_h2: Without the 1 MΩ resistor it beeps even with a dry probe – that's how sensitive the circuit is.
exp_4_13_erklaerung: T1 amplifies the tiny current from the probe, T2 amplifies the result again. Together that makes about 200 × 200 = 40,000 – so much that even the dry probe would be enough. That's why the 1 MΩ resistor leads the smallest current past the base to 0V. This circuit is called a Darlington pair; it's also what's inside the amplifier module.
exp_4_13_mehr: This circuit was invented by Sidney Darlington in 1953.
exp_4_13_w1: Move the drop one field further away. Does it still beep?
exp_4_13_echt: In touch switches the tiny current through a finger is enough – thanks to amplifiers like this.
exp_4_14_frage: In the bathroom the fan keeps running for a while after you switch off the light. Can the timer module control a motor like that?
exp_4_14_v2: No, modules can't drive a motor.
exp_4_14_b1: After one press the motor runs for a few seconds and then stops.
exp_4_14_b2: The motor doesn't run at all.
exp_4_14_b3: The motor runs all the time.
exp_4_14_s1: Power the timer module: +9V to M1, M2 to 0V.
exp_4_14_s2: Push button A1–A2, +9V at A1, A2 to the input "start" (M3).
exp_4_14_s3: Motor long on B3–B5, +9V at B3, B5 to the output "aus" (M4). Press briefly.
exp_4_14_h1: The timer module's output switches the path to 0V – like the stairwell light.
exp_4_14_h2: The motor takes the place of the LED.
exp_4_14_loesung: +9V → M1, M2 → 0V, +9V → A1, button A1–A2, A2 → M3 (start), +9V → B3, motor B3–B5, B5 → M4 (aus).
exp_4_14_erklaerung: The timer module's output transistor switches the motor just like an LED – it copes with the bigger current too. That gives a run-on: a short push, then it runs for a while.
exp_4_14_mehr: Inside the timer module are a 100 µF capacitor and a 47 kΩ resistor: 0.69 × 47 kΩ × 100 µF ≈ 3.2 seconds.
exp_4_14_w1: Replace the motor with the buzzer. Does it become a kitchen timer?
exp_4_14_echt: Bathroom fans, computer cooling fans and stairwell lights have a run-on time.
exp_4_15_frage: The amplifier module should switch on the blinker module as soon as water comes. Can one module switch another module?
exp_4_15_b1: When the probe is wet, the LED blinks.
exp_4_15_s1: Amplifier module in M1–M4 (+9V at M1, M2 to 0V), blinker module in M6–M9 (+9V at M6).
exp_4_15_s2: Minus of the blinker module (M7) to the amplifier output (M4). Probe long C1–C3, +9V at C1, C3 to the input (M3).
exp_4_15_s3: 470 Ω B6–B7 (+9V at B6), LED B7–C7, C7 to the blinker output (M8). Water drop on the probe.
exp_4_15_h1: The amplifier switches the blinker module's minus connection.
exp_4_15_h2: Without water the blinker module gets no current.
exp_4_15_erklaerung: Here the amplifier module is the switch for the blinker module's power: only when water lets a small current into its input does it connect the blinker module to 0V – then the LED blinks. Modules can be combined like building blocks.
exp_4_15_mehr: With "Look inside" both modules you can see how the transistors work together.
exp_4_15_w1: Also connect the piezo to the blinker output. Does it become an alarm you can hear too?
exp_4_15_echt: Real alarm systems are made of building blocks: sensor, amplifier, timer, lamp and horn.
